Comptroller Christine Stevenson has been in Europe recently for a series of engagements, supported by Customs’ London-based Counsellor, Simon Jones.

In Lisbon, Portugal, Christine met with the Maritime Analysis and Operations Centre to discuss global maritime drug smuggling trends, and visited the European Union Drugs Agency, which provides strategic analysis on emerging drug threats.

These relationships help Customs stay connected to global trends, strengthen drug disruption efforts, and support the security of New Zealand’s border.

Read further: https://lnkd.in/edaMy5Ps","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/nzcustoms_partner-agencies-of-the-newly-formed-illicit-activity-7477934182640484353-c0ZB"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"New Zealand Customs Service","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/nzcustoms"},"datePublished":"2026-06-29T23:06:39.515Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/nzcustoms_a-30-year-old-auckland-man-was-sentenced-activity-7477497795197865984-cvTy","text":"A 30 year-old Auckland man was sentenced in the Manukau District Court yesterday (29 June 2026) to three years and seven months’ imprisonment after he was arrested by Customs officers and charged with importing, possessing and distributing objectionable publications. He was automatically registered as a Child Sex Offender.

The man arrived at Auckland International Airport on 14 February 2025 following a trip to Australia. Customs officers had identified him as a risk for online child sexual abuse material offending and located a total of 385 files depicting child sexual abuse in a protected application on his phone. He was arrested at the airport by officers from Customs’ Child Exploitation Operations Team and charged with importing objectionable publications.

Further forensic analysis of the man’s phone identified that since 2020 he had used multiple online accounts to store and share at least 754 objectionable files, all but one showing the sexual abuse of real children. The material included distressing videos involving infants, and totalled approximately 33 hours of footage.

In the first six months of 2026, Customs has charged fifteen people with importing or exporting offences involving objectionable publications, among other related charges. This is the same number of arrests Customs made for the same offending across the whole of 2025.

Chief Customs Officer - Child Exploitation Operations Team, Simon Peterson, said "Anyone intercepted moving such material across our borders, whether physically on devices or via the internet, should not be mistaken for being caught merely in possession of undesirable material: these are real children being terribly abused. 

Importing or exporting child sexual abuse material across our borders contributes significantly to the global proliferation of this deeply troubling offending. This re-victimises those vulnerable children in the material who suffered the recorded abuse, and creates a sinister demand for more material, and more victims."

If you have concerns or suspicions about someone who may be trading in or producing child sexual abuse images or videos, contact Customs confidentially on 0800 WE PROTECT (0800 937 768) or Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111. If you are, or know of, someone who is at risk or being abused, contact the Police immediately.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/nzcustoms_a-30-year-old-auckland-man-was-sentenced-activity-7477497795197865984-cvTy"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"New Zealand Customs Service","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/nzcustoms"},"datePublished":"2026-06-26T01:50:19.077Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/nzcustoms_worlddrugday-activity-7476089429850353664-JBlI","text":"Today (26 June), New Zealand Customs marks the International Day Against Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking.

This year’s global message highlights the need to tackle the ongoing challenges of drug smuggling through innovation and strong cooperation. 

Illicit drugs don’t just harm individuals — they fuel organised crime, damage communities, and create real risks at our border and beyond. Globally, the drug trade continues to evolve, with transnational, serious and organised criminal (TSOC) groups using new methods to target communities and expand their reach. 

Customs works alongside domestic and international partners every day to detect and stop drugs entering New Zealand, disrupt criminal networks, and protect our communities. 

By working together — across borders and across communities — we can strengthen our response.

If you suspect or know of possible drug smuggling, you can report it by calling 0800 WE PROTECT (0800 937 768) in confidence or Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

Aged between 22 and 25, six couriers and organisers have appeared in the Manukau District Court, charged with the importation of a Class A controlled drug - methamphetamine. Customs alleges they were collectively involved in smuggling an estimated 93 kilograms of methamphetamine inside suitcases, on return trips from Malaysia.

Customs Investigations Manager, Dominic Adams, says the recruitment of young drug couriers is an active and dangerous development, with transnational, serious and organised crime groups turning to social media platforms for exploitative purposes.

“Criminal groups are using social media to entice our young people into high-risk illegal activities, with the promise of overseas travel, cash and an Insta-worthy lifestyle.”

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">A 30 year-old Auckland man was sentenced in the Manukau District Court yesterday (29 June 2026) to three years and seven months’ imprisonment after he was arrested by Customs officers and charged with importing, possessing and distributing objectionable publications. He was automatically registered as a Child Sex Offender.

The man arrived at Auckland International Airport on 14 February 2025 following a trip to Australia. Customs officers had identified him as a risk for online child sexual abuse material offending and located a total of 385 files depicting child sexual abuse in a protected application on his phone. He was arrested at the airport by officers from Customs’ Child Exploitation Operations Team and charged with importing objectionable publications.

Further forensic analysis of the man’s phone identified that since 2020 he had used multiple online accounts to store and share at least 754 objectionable files, all but one showing the sexual abuse of real children. The material included distressing videos involving infants, and totalled approximately 33 hours of footage.

In the first six months of 2026, Customs has charged fifteen people with importing or exporting offences involving objectionable publications, among other related charges. This is the same number of arrests Customs made for the same offending across the whole of 2025.

Chief Customs Officer - Child Exploitation Operations Team, Simon Peterson, said "Anyone intercepted moving such material across our borders, whether physically on devices or via the internet, should not be mistaken for being caught merely in possession of undesirable material: these are real children being terribly abused. 

Importing or exporting child sexual abuse material across our borders contributes significantly to the global proliferation of this deeply troubling offending. This re-victimises those vulnerable children in the material who suffered the recorded abuse, and creates a sinister demand for more material, and more victims."

If you have concerns or suspicions about someone who may be trading in or producing child sexual abuse images or videos, contact Customs confidentially on 0800 WE PROTECT (0800 937 768) or Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111. If you are, or know of, someone who is at risk or being abused, contact the Police immediately.</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Today (26 June), New Zealand Customs marks the International Day Against Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking.

This year’s global message highlights the need to tackle the ongoing challenges of drug smuggling through innovation and strong cooperation. 

Illicit drugs don’t just harm individuals — they fuel organised crime, damage communities, and create real risks at our border and beyond. Globally, the drug trade continues to evolve, with transnational, serious and organised criminal (TSOC) groups using new methods to target communities and expand their reach. 

Customs works alongside domestic and international partners every day to detect and stop drugs entering New Zealand, disrupt criminal networks, and protect our communities. 

By working together — across borders and across communities — we can strengthen our response.

If you suspect or know of possible drug smuggling, you can report it by calling 0800 WE PROTECT (0800 937 768) in confidence or Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

  <div class="attributed-text-segment-list__container relative mt-1 mb-1.5 babybear:mt-0 babybear:mb-0.5">
    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Six young New Zealanders are before the courts following a major Customs investigation into a drug syndicate recruiting couriers through social media.

Aged between 22 and 25, six couriers and organisers have appeared in the Manukau District Court, charged with the importation of a Class A controlled drug - methamphetamine. Customs alleges they were collectively involved in smuggling an estimated 93 kilograms of methamphetamine inside suitcases, on return trips from Malaysia.

Customs Investigations Manager, Dominic Adams, says the recruitment of young drug couriers is an active and dangerous development, with transnational, serious and organised crime groups turning to social media platforms for exploitative purposes.

“Criminal groups are using social media to entice our young people into high-risk illegal activities, with the promise of overseas travel, cash and an Insta-worthy lifestyle.”

Read more: <a class="link" href="https://lnkd.in/eW3YrJAf?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://lnkd.in/eW3YrJAf</a>

Everyone has a role to play in protecting New Zealand’s border and communities from illicit drugs. Suspicions about drug smuggling can be reported by calling 0800 WE PROTECT (0800 937 768) in confidence, or Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">This National Volunteer Week, we’re recognising the incredible support of <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/christchurch-international-airport-limited?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Christchurch International Airport Limited</a>'s  Ambassador programme — and the difference volunteers like Lynley and Cheryl make every day.
